title: Full-Stack High-Volume Quantum Networking Architecture based on Photonic-Integrated Tin Vacancy Centers in Diamond
authors: Hamza Raniwala, Ian Christen, Helaman Flores, David Starling, Ryan Murphy, Eric Bersin, Kevin Chen, Marc Davis, Maxim Sirotin, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Ethan G. Arnault, Matthew E. Trusheim, P. B. Dixon, Dirk R. Englund
abstract: Solid state quantum emitters are a leading platform for photonic quantum networking with memory nodes. However, the inhomogeneous distribution of quantum emitters, as well as several environmental factors (i.e. strain and electric fields) spread the frequency spectrum of the qubits, making them distinguishable and therefore not a reliable resource for distributed quantum entanglement. In this paper, we demonstrate a full-stack approach to integrating nearly indistinguishable tin vacancy (SnV$^-$) quantum emitters on a frequency-tunable photonic interposer that overcomes the native distribution and static variation of quantum emitters for an indistinguishable photonic quantum networking platform. We demonstrate a silicon nitride-on-insulator photonic integrated circuit (PIC) with accompanying multiphysics digital twin (MPhDT) that guides discovery of SnV$^-$ strain-tuning parameters and informs construction of a multi-channel quantum repeater node. On this node, we achieve the first simultaneous demonstration of spectral tuning of the zero phonon line (ZPL) at GHz scale; coherent electron spin control with gate times of $<80$ ns; strongly- and weakly-coupled nuclear spin detection; and commercial fiber array-coupled readout of a SnV$^-$ center. Finally, we propose and simulate improvements to the architecture that achieve 99.96% connectivity of $ N \sim 1000$ emitters spanning the inhomogeneous distribution of SnV$^-$ centers in strained diamond, where distributed quantum entanglement may be realized.
summary: The paper presents a breakthrough 'full-stack' architecture integrating SnV- emitters into photonic chips for quantum networking. By coupling experimental measurements with a Multiphysics Digital Twin, the authors successfully characterized strain effects and demonstrated simultaneous control over spectral tuning, electron spin, and nuclear spins. This work establishes a robust platform roadmap toward realizing large-scale, high-connectivity quantum repeaters.
main_problem: Scaling solid-state quantum emitters for distributed quantum entanglement is limited by emitter frequency inhomogeneity, environmental variations, and difficulty in achieving scalable coherent control.
main_result: The authors demonstrated a full-stack architecture enabling simultaneous spectral tuning, spin readout, and nuclear spin control, proposing a roadmap to achieve high connectivity ($N \sim 1000$) for quantum repeaters.
method: A combination of experimental characterization (strain mapping, spin echo measurements) and advanced computational modeling using a Multiphysics Digital Twin (MPhDT) guided by Expectation-Maximization algorithms was employed.
model_or_system: The platform integrates SnV- quantum emitters in diamond nanophotonic microchiplets (QMC) onto a frequency-tunable silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit (PIC). The MPhDT simulates electro-mechanical strain effects on the emitter's zero phonon line (ZPL) frequency.
key_observables: GHz scale spectral tuning of ZPL, electron spin coherence time ($T_2 \sim 1	ext{ms}$), and measurable coupling efficiency between waveguides.
important_parameters: Strain susceptibilities ($t_{\perp}, t_{\|}$), gate times ($<80\ 	ext{ns}$), and target connectivity of $99.96\%$ for large emitter arrays.
main_assumptions: The ability to model the complex interplay between strain, electric fields, and quantum emitter properties using coupled FEM/FDTD simulations is assumed for predictive control.
figures_summary: Figures likely detail spectral tuning curves vs. voltage, spin echo decay plots (XY8 sequences), and simulation results showing achievable connectivity based on overlap criteria.
paper_structure: The work progresses from identifying the limitations of current solid-state platforms to proposing a full-stack architecture ($	ext{QR-PIC}$), detailing the use of $	ext{MPhDT}$ for parameter extraction, demonstrating advanced control (spin/spectral tuning), and finally simulating scalability for large networks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges in solid-state quantum networking by providing a comprehensive, multi-physics framework to overcome emitter disorder and enable scalable entanglement distribution.
